Tilicho · AI-SDLC Orchestrator · Claude Code harness

One run, end to end — from two prompts to a costed, human-gated build.

A field engineer opens Claude Code in an empty folder and types two things. Fifty-five minutes later there is a working Express service, a passing test suite, a security review, four human approvals and a per-phase cost table. Twelve frames from that run, in order, with the numbers reconciled against the run record rather than the screen.

The run, frame by frame

Timestamps are from the screenshots themselves. The chip on each frame says which tier was doing the work at that moment — the premium tier judging, the mechanical tier building, or a human deciding.

01
11:44:39 PM
Human

Prompt 1, in an empty folder

Nothing is cloned and no command is typed. The whole install is one sentence with a repo URL. Claude Code reads the repo's own SETUP.md, registers the marketplace, installs the plugin and builds the bundled model server. The permission card is the harness asking before it touches the network — the run has not started and nothing has been spent.

02
12:00:32 AM
Human

Install verified, and honest about it

Marketplace tilicho-ai-labs at head f7c6185, plugin multi-model-orchestrator@0.2.4, bundled server built, verify-setup.mjs --fix exits clean. Note the wording on screen: the marketplace and plugin were already registered here and steps 1–2 were already done. This machine had run the install before, so this frame shows a verified install, not a first-time one.

03
12:02:33 AM
Human

Routing shown before a rupee is spent

/sdlc-run states the policy as fact, read from the policy file rather than recited: judgment phases to claude-opus-4-7, mechanical phases to gemini-3.5-flash, with both sets of per-million rates on screen. Debug starts on Flash and escalates to Opus after two failures; anything unrecognised fails safe to Opus. With no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY present it recommends estimated telemetry and says plainly what that costs in accuracy. Then it asks for a yes.

04
12:06:14 AM
Opus

Gate 1 — requirements

The first of four human gates. The options are specific, not ceremonial: approve as written, revise FR-7 so a wrong method returns 405 instead of 404, revise something else, or abort — and the abort option quotes the exact sunk cost, $0.0728. The side panel carries the instruction the orchestrator is running under: Do not self-approve any gate.

05
12:10:06 AM
Opus

Gate 2 — architecture

The design phase surfaces two decisions rather than burying them. The 404 catch-all is a path-less app.use, not app.all('*'), which is what makes 404-on-POST /ping fall out for free — and which pins Express to ^4.19.2, because v5 changed wildcard path parsing. HEAD /ping returns 200 with an empty body via Express's automatic HEAD handling; no requirement covers it, and the architect left it deliberately so the call belongs to a human. Cost so far: $0.2472 across two phases.

06
12:19:46 AM
Flash

Gate 2 approved → handoff to Flash

The moment the routing becomes real. Gate 2 is approved and codegen and tests dispatch to Gemini Flash from here. Two agents are live in the background panel at once — the pipeline itself and the senior code review — while the main session stays responsive.

07
12:32:43 AM
Flash

Mechanical tier working in parallel

Seven finished background tasks: architecture design, senior code review, security review, dependency install and test suite, a live server boot, and a curl probe of the acceptance criteria. Five task packets were dispatched concurrently. This concurrency is also why the run records zero cache hits — see the caveats below.

08
12:34:43 AM
Opus

Gate 3 — security review

The reviewer found one defect worth attention (F-01): src/app.js:21 passes an attacker-influenced err.status straight to res.status(), which throws inside the error handler and unwinds to Express's default handler — HTML plus a stack trace with absolute host paths. It is not reachable today, so it is a latent defect in a guarantee, not an exploitable bug. Probes were run for real: ?x=<script>, a 30 KB URL, TRACE, OPTIONS, a 1 MB POST — all returned the identical 21-byte JSON 404. And an honesty note: PII and audit-log items are recorded not applicable, not passing.

The $0.9218 across 7 phases on this screen is a faulty interim display. The reconciled total is $0.8413 — telemetry.jsonl sums to it exactly and manifest.json records cost_usd = 0.84132. Quote $0.8413.
09
12:37:24 AM
Opus

Gate 4 — the numbers, per phase

The run is complete: $0.8413, six files, 2/2 tests passing. Every phase is broken out into cached input, fresh input and output, with the model it actually ran on and the provenance of the figure — estimated or vendor — in its own column rather than in a footnote.

10
12:37:28 AM
Flash

Routing, made visible

Five Opus calls carry 86.0% of the cost; six Flash calls carry 14.0% — and every one of the six shipped files was written by the mechanical tier. The premium tier decided what to build and judged the result but wrote none of it. The orchestrator is deliberately careful about the savings claim in the text below the table; that wording is reproduced in the caveats.

11
12:37:32 AM
Human

Verification, run for real

npm install exit 0 · npm test 2/2 with no open handles · npm start listening on 3000 · GET /ping → 200 with a parseable ISO-8601 time · GET /nope and POST /ping → 404 JSON, 21 bytes, no HTML · npm audit 0 vulnerabilities. One deviation is stated rather than hidden: the workflow calls for a SUMMARY.md, but this session's harness blocks subagents from writing report files, so it is absent — and run_record.files was corrected so the manifest does not claim a file that is not on disk.

12

Manifest finalised — run done

gates.gate_4_final is accepted. Ping Service · policy opus-plus-flash · telemetry estimated · $0.8413 · 11 calls · 6 files · 2/2 tests green · four gates, all human-approved. Code in src/, run record in .sdlc/. Elapsed: 55 minutes from the first prompt.
